opus-5.5.text:
I think this is something a lot of people in academia are anxious about right now, and I understand why. If you look at the past few years, many of the headline results, the large language models and the big multimodal systems, came out of industry labs with enormous compute budgets. So it's natural to ask whether universities still matter.

My view is that academia's role hasn't disappeared, but it has changed, and maybe it's become even more important in some ways. Companies are very good at scaling something once the direction is clear. When there's a recipe that works, they can throw thousands of GPUs at it and push it much further than any university lab could. But scaling a known recipe is not the same as finding the next recipe. A lot of the foundational ideas we rely on today, in architectures, in representation learning, in how we think about vision, came from small groups trying things that didn't obviously make sense at the time.

So I think academia should resist the temptation to just compete on the same axis. If a university lab tries to train a slightly smaller version of what a big company already has, that's usually not a good use of time. You'll lose that race. What academia can do is ask questions that aren't immediately tied to a product roadmap. For example, I care a lot about visual understanding and about whether our models really understand the world, not just language about the world. There's still a big gap there, and I don't think the answer is simply "more data, more parameters." That kind of question, where you're not sure the payoff will come in six months, is where academic freedom really matters.

Another role is being honest and critical. Industry has incentives, which is fine, but it means certain things get emphasized and others don't. Academia can do careful evaluation, point out where models fail, open up things that are closed, and train students to think independently. That last part is maybe the most underrated. The people who will set the direction ten years from now are students today, and how we train them to have taste, to pick problems, to not just follow the hype, that's a long-term contribution companies can't easily replace.

Of course, compute is a real problem, and I don't want to pretend it isn't. I think we need better collaboration models, between universities and industry, and also public investment in shared compute. But even with limited resources, I'm fairly optimistic. Constraints often push you toward more creative ideas. Some of the most interesting work comes exactly from people who couldn't afford to brute-force the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes academia’s role in pursuing independent questions and shaping future research, but it does not identify setting the research agenda as academia’s traditional social responsibility.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because the ground has shifted so much in just a few years. When I was a PhD student, academia was still where most of the foundational ideas came from. Now, if you look at where the biggest models are being trained, where the compute is, where the data is, it's almost entirely inside a handful of companies. So the first thing I'd say is, we should be honest about that. Academia is not going to win the scaling game. We don't have the GPUs, and pretending otherwise just leads to a lot of frustration and a lot of papers that are basically small-scale imitations of what industry already did.

But I actually don't think that means academia has lost its role in setting direction. I think the role has changed. If industry is optimizing the current paradigm, then academia's job is to question the paradigm. The incentive structures are completely different. A company has a product, it has a roadmap, it has shareholders. Once something works, the rational thing to do is to pour everything into making it work better. That's not a criticism, it's just how it goes. But that also means there's very little room inside those organizations to say, wait, maybe this whole approach has a ceiling, maybe we should look at something that won't pay off for five years.

That's where I think universities still matter enormously. We can afford to be wrong. We can afford to work on things that look unfashionable. A lot of what I care about, for example understanding representations, asking what visual models actually learn, whether the way we think about vision and language is even the right framing, those questions don't need ten thousand GPUs. They need careful thinking and good experimental design. And some of the most influential ideas in the field, if you trace them back, started as somewhat strange academic projects that nobody in industry would have greenlit at the time.

The other thing I'd emphasize is people. Academia's biggest output is not papers, it's students. Every person who goes into one of these labs was trained somewhere, and the taste they develop, what problems they think are interesting, how they evaluate evidence, how skeptical they are of hype, that's shaped in grad school. So in a very real sense, academia is still setting direction, just with a longer delay. The researchers who will decide what the field looks like in ten years are in seminar rooms right now.

What worries me is not that companies are leading. It's that academia might respond by trying to compete on their terms and losing its own identity. If every university lab is chasing the same benchmarks with a tenth of the resources, that's the worst of both worlds. I'd much rather see us lean into what we're actually good at: slower, deeper, more contrarian work, and being the place where the field's conscience lives, where people can openly say the emperor has no clothes if that's what the evidence shows.

So, to summarize, I'd say academia's role now is less about leading the frontier and more about defining what the frontier should be. And I think that's actually a pretty important job.

r001.rationale: The response says academia historically produced foundational ideas and describes its role as setting research direction and defining what the frontier should be.

astra-6.text:
I think academia still has a very important role, but we have to be thoughtful about what that role is. If a university lab tries to compete with a large company on exactly the same problem, using exactly the same approach, but with a fraction of the compute, that’s a difficult position to be in.

The opportunity is to ask questions that companies may not have the incentive to ask. Is the direction everyone is pursuing actually the right one? Can we test an idea at a smaller scale that changes how we think about the problem? What are we missing when we focus on a particular benchmark?

Setting the direction doesn’t necessarily mean building the largest model. It can mean introducing a new way to frame a problem, or producing a convincing experiment that challenges an assumption. Academia should be a place where students have the freedom to do that, including the freedom to fail. If we just follow the road maps of the big companies, we give up a lot of what makes academic research valuable.

r001.rationale: The response describes academia’s role in shaping research direction, but does not identify setting the research agenda as academia’s traditional social responsibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academia still has a very important role, but we have to be thoughtful about what that role is. If a university lab defines success as doing the same thing as a large company, just with one percent of the compute, that’s a difficult position to be in. We should ask what questions we can pursue that aren’t being prioritized inside those companies.

There’s a difference between leading in capability and setting the direction of research. Companies can push capabilities very quickly because they have the resources and the engineering infrastructure. But academia can question the assumptions behind that progress. Are we measuring the right things? Do we understand why a method works? Is there a different approach that looks uncompetitive today but could become important later?

That freedom is valuable. A student should be able to spend time on an uncertain idea without having to explain how it improves a product next quarter. Of course, academic researchers also face pressure to publish, so we have to protect that freedom ourselves.

I don’t think the answer is for academia to abandon large-scale research, either. Access to compute matters. But our ambition shouldn’t be limited to keeping up. It should be to produce ideas, understanding, and researchers who can change what the whole field decides to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says academia can develop ideas that change what the field works on, but it does not identify setting the research agenda as academia’s traditional social responsibility.
